results.title: Latency and why it's matters. Latency != Response time | by Ninad Desai | Medium
results.content: * **P50**: The median latency, meaning 50% of requests are faster than this time, and 50% are slower. For example, if your P95 latency is 200 ms, it means that 95% of the time, your system responds within 200 milliseconds, but 5% of requests take longer, possibly much longer. **Tail latency** refers to the **latency of the slowest requests** in a system, typically the **highest percentiles** (like P99, P99.9). * **Definition**: P50 latency is the value at which 50% of the requests are faster, and 50% are slower. * **Definition**: P95 is the latency value below which 95% of requests are complete. * **Use Case**: This percentile focuses on **tail latency**, helping you understand how your system handles the **worst-performing** requests. * **Definition**: P99 is the latency value below which 99% of requests complete, leaving just 1% of the requests slower than this value. * **Use Case**: This percentile is used in **ultra-low-latency** systems, like financial trading platforms or mission-critical applications, where even the smallest percentage of slow requests is unacceptable.

results.title: Why do we talk about P99 and P95 request latency? - shiplog
results.content: # Why do we talk about P99 and P95 request latency? When we talk about a value being the P99 (or P95, or P), that means that 99% of the time, requests finish in this time or less. More concretely, if the P99 request latency for your site is 1s, then 99% of requests take 1s or less. So, if we talk about P50 request latency, there is only a 50% chance that requests take less than that amount of time - there will be *a lot* of customers for whom it takes longer to load the site. results.title: Understanding p50 p75 p90 p95 and p99 latency metrics
results.content: Imagine you’re at a busy restaurant, and you want to know how long it takes for people to receive their food after ordering. * Latency: This is the total time from when you place your order to when the food is served. * p50 (50th percentile): This is the median—half the people get their food faster than this, and half the people wait longer. Example: Out of 100 customers, 50 people get their food in less time than this, and the other 50 wait longer. So, if p50 = 15 minutes, it means that half of all the orders are served in 15 minutes or less. * p75 (75th percentile): This is the point where 75% of the people get their food faster than this, and 25% of people have to wait longer. Example: If p75 = 20 minutes, it means that 75% of the people got their food in 20 minutes or less, and 25% waited longer. * p90 (90th percentile): This means 90% of the customers got their food in this time, and 10% waited longer. Example: If p90 = 25 minutes, 90% of customers were served in 25 minutes or less, but 10% had to wait longer. * p95 (95th percentile): This is similar to p90 but for an even higher percentage—95% of the people were served in this time, and 5% waited longer. Example: If p95 = 30 minutes, it means 95% of people got their food in 30 minutes or less, and only 5% waited longer. * p99 (99th percentile): This is the top 1%. It’s the maximum time that still only 1% of people had to wait longer than. Example: If p99 = 40 minutes, it means 99% of the people got their food in 40 minutes or less, and only 1% waited longer. These values give you a sense of how most people are being served and how much the slowest people are waiting:. * Only 1% of the people had to wait longer than 40 minutes. * If you look at p99, you can see that there’s a small group of people who experience much longer wait times.

Welcome to the wild world of **latency percentiles -** where the average lies, and the truth hides in the tail. ### Why Averages Don’t Tell the Full Story. Let’s say you run a food delivery app. > *“Our average delivery time is 28 minutes. In software too, averages gloss over **spikes**, **timeouts**, and **weird edge cases** that only happen under load, or on slow networks, or for that one unlucky user in a corner of the world. That’s where **p50**, **p95**, and **p99** come in. * **p50 (Median)** - 50% of requests are faster than this. * **p95 -** 95% of requests are faster. * **p99 -** 99% of requests are faster. The value at the `I`-th position in the sorted array is your percentile latency. If p95 checkout latency jumps from 400ms to 3s, it won’t show up in the average — but it **kills conversion.**. If p99 response times are creeping up, engineers integrating with it will feel the pain and start building retries, timeouts, or worse: **workarounds**. * **p50:** Good for a sanity check - the median user. * **p90/p95:** What most users feel. One in a hundred - often the loudest voice in your support queue. * **p100:** Literally the slowest request. * Percentiles tell you what your users are actually experiencing. * p95 and p99 help you catch latency spikes and user pain before it explodes. When it comes to performance, *how fast you are on average* matters a lot less than *how slow you are at your worst*.
